title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1; preregistration manifest SHA-256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891) that evaluated whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs were analysed after preregistered exclusions (34 both‑arm provider failures excluded; see deterministic reconciliation artifacts). Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. The exact McNemar test was the preregistered primary hypothesis test and decision rule; a paired bootstrap percentile interval (B=10,000; seed=1729) is reported as a descriptive supplementary estimator (95% CI = [0.0037593985, 0.0375939850]) and is explicitly not used to overturn the preregistered significance decision. Repair was invoked for 6 episodes; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode timing was not archived and the preregistered latency estimand could not be evaluated. All execution and analysis artifacts (raw responses, validator traces, provider accounting, and reconciliation manifests) are archived to support reanalysis. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate estimand the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for network operations (NetOps) activities such as intent→CLI translation, automated configuration synthesis, and maintenance workflows [1,2]. Stochastic LLM outputs can omit required commands, violate ordering constraints, or otherwise produce semantics that threaten operational safety. A pragmatic mitigation pattern is generate–verify–repair (GVR): (1) generate a candidate configuration with an LLM, (2) deterministically verify it with a network verifier (e.g., Batfish or header‑space analysis), and (3) when the verifier flags defects, use a bounded repair loop to produce a corrected candidate. Prior proposals and prototypes argue this architecture can provide deterministic acceptance criteria for stochastic agents [3,4] but large‑scale, preregistered paired evaluations that archive verifier traces and quantify verifier‑triggered repair benefit on reproducible NetOps task banks remain limited. This work reports a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment that measures the incremental effect of a verifier‑triggered, bounded automated repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics: the identical single sampled initial LLM candidate per task is used for both baseline and guarded outcomes, and the guarded arm may invoke at most one automated LLM repair if the initial candidate fails the deterministic validator. The principal contribution is a reproducible paired evaluation with exact paired counts, preregistered inferential procedures, deterministic validator semantics, and representative artifact‑grounded repair examples.
sections.related_work: LLM applications in NetOps cover intent‑to‑configuration generation, zero‑touch management, and AIOps orchestration [1,2]. Benchmarks such as NetConfEval evaluate translation ability and reveal vendor‑dialect, sequencing, and constraint challenges for unconstrained generation [1]. Surveys and systematic reviews document hallucination, constraint violations, and brittleness as recurring failure modes and advocate grounding and verifier integration [2]. Generate–verify‑repair architectures have been proposed in adjacent domains (notably code generation and regulated document production) to combine stochastic generation with deterministic oracles and bounded repair logic to improve correctness reproducibility [3]. Network verifiers (Batfish, header‑space analyses and related tooling) provide concrete, automatable checks for reachability and ordering constraints and are natural oracles for GVR pipelines, but these verifiers have finite rule coverage and entail engineering tradeoffs that affect outcomes [4,5]. Our study differs by executing a preregistered paired test under shared_initial_candidate semantics, archiving validator traces for every episode, and reporting exact contingency counts together with the preregistered exact McNemar test and a supplementary paired bootstrap CI to characterize effect magnitude.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment followed preregistration cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Shared_initial_candidate semantics (executed exactly as preregistered) means: for each task a single sampled initial model candidate was produced and recorded; the baseline outcome is that candidate scored by the deterministic validator; the guarded outcome reuses that identical recorded candidate and, only if that candidate failed, may trigger at most one additional guarded repair call. This design isolates the effect of a verifier‑triggered, bounded repair for a fixed initial draw and matches the preregistered execution contract (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate"). We emphasize that the design does not measure independent multi‑draw or constrained‑prompt first‑pass effects, which would require separate preregistered arms and independent initial samples.

Task bank, sampling, and inclusion rules: The preregistered task bank combined public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator to produce 300 intent→CLI pairs stratified into two vendor‑dialect clusters (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like). Inclusion/exclusion rules followed the preregistration: exact public duplicates detected by the contamination check would be excluded from the primary analysis (none were excluded for exact duplication in this execution); transient provider/API failures triggered up to two automatic retries; pairs where both arms failed due to infrastructure/model API errors were excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule. The deterministic reconciliation artifact records the applied exclusions and accounting (see Results and reconciliation artifact SHA below).

Model orchestration, stage semantics, and provider accounting: The declared model used for generation and any repair calls was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). To address reviewer concerns about stage/condition accounting semantics we explicitly define the recorded provider/stage fields and present the run counts (all values archived in the evidence bundle):
- shared_initial_generation: the single sampled initial candidate produced per task (stage_counts recorded = 300). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics this same candidate is reused to score both baseline and guarded outcomes; no independent separate baseline/guarded first‑pass generations were invoked.
- repair: additional model calls invoked only when the shared initial candidate failed the deterministic validator (stage_counts recorded = 6). These repair calls are the only model events that produce new candidate content for a guarded outcome; otherwise the guarded outcome is the re‑score of the shared initial candidate.
- hosted_model_call_event_count = 306 (total model‑call events recorded across the run), completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34. Provider accounting and stage_counts are reconciled in the deterministic_reconciliation artifact (see SHA below). The explicit staging semantics above avoid misinterpretation of stage_counts or condition_counts as independent per‑arm first‑pass generation counts.

Deterministic validator and scoring: The binary oracle deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executed a fixed rule battery per episode: (1) syntactic CLI parsing and normalization; (2) required‑sequence checks against the task's required_sequence; (3) constrained‑field touch checks against allowed_touched_fields and allowed_fields; (4) reachability and topology‑dependent constraints computed on the seeded synthetic topology (a Batfish‑style evaluation). Each validator trace archives parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, normalized_configuration and a boolean valid flag. The primary binary endpoint used the preregistered scoring rule 'full_intent_constraint_validation' recorded in the per‑episode scoring artifacts.

Repair loop bounding and prompts: Per preregistration the automated repair stage was strictly bounded to at most one LLM repair call per episode when the initial candidate failed. Repair prompts were constructed from the task payload, the validator failure diagnostics, and an instruction to return a corrected configuration satisfying the task constraints; all repair prompts, repaired outputs, and subsequent validator traces are archived for the 6 invoked repairs.

Inferential procedures and primary decision rule: The preregistered primary hypothesis test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes at α = 0.05 (estimator id paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Interval estimation was prespecified as a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B = 10,000; seed = 1729) reported as a descriptive supplementary estimator. We explicitly report the exact McNemar p‑value as the preregistered decision result and present the bootstrap CI as a descriptive interval that complements magnitude interpretation; the bootstrap CI is not used to overturn the preregistered hypothesis decision. Missingness handling for the primary analysis followed the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule: pairs with both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures were excluded from the confirmatory McNemar test. The deterministic reconciliation artifact records the excluded both‑arm episodes and reconciles model call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json; SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490).
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The preregistered plan targeted 300 tasks (600 episodes). The run recorded planned_episode_count = 600 and completed_episode_count = 532; provider/infrastructure transient failures produced failed_episode_count = 68. Applying the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' exclusion rule (exclude both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures) produced complete_pairs = 266 analysed in the primary test; the deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact documents these exclusions (SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490). Provider accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34; stage_counts recorded shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6.

Primary paired outcomes: For the 266 complete pairs the episode‑level validator outcomes yield contingency counts n11 = 260 (both baseline and guarded pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). These counts give baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090 and guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015; the paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.01879699248. Applying the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test to the discordant counts (n10 = 5, n01 = 0) produced p = 0.0625. By the preregistered decision rule (α = 0.05) this result does not reject the null hypothesis of no paired difference.

Supplementary interval estimate and bootstrap: As prespecified, a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B = 10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) was computed and returned 95% CI = [0.0037593985, 0.0375939850]. We report this CI as a descriptive summary of effect magnitude and uncertainty alongside the preregistered McNemar decision, noting that the discrete exact test is conservative with few discordants while the bootstrap CI summarizes empirical resampling variability.

Repair invocation and operational yield: Repair was invoked in 6 episodes (stage_counts: repair = 6). The discordant pattern (n10 = 5) indicates at most five analysed repairs converted a failing initial candidate into a guarded pass among the complete pairs. Median repair iterations per analysed pair = 0 because most tasks required no repair. A descriptive number‑needed‑to‑treat (NNT) computed as 1 / absolute_risk_reduction = 1 / 0.01879699248 ≈ 53.2 describes that, under these run conditions and shared_initial_candidate semantics, roughly 53 guarded tasks were associated with one additional verifier‑approved configuration relative to baseline; this scalar is descriptive and conditional on the observed high baseline pass rate.

Representative repair example: Representative archived artifacts illustrate typical failure and repair behavior. Task‑000008 (difficulty labeled "extreme" in the task manifest) had a shared initial candidate with a truncated final token and a parsed_command_count shortfall; the automated repair call produced a completed sequence that satisfied required_command_count and resolved the validator violation_count to 0. Per‑episode validator traces (scoring JSONs) include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation codes, and the valid boolean and are archived for audit and reanalysis.

Sensitivity to missingness: Thirty‑four both‑arm episodes were excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule; including those 34 episodes conservatively as failures yields baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667 and guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333 but leaves the observed discordant pair counts for the analysed subset unchanged and therefore does not alter the preregistered McNemar p = 0.0625 for the analysed complete pairs. The reconciliation artifact documents these exclusions (deterministic_reconciliation.json; SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490).

Reproducibility pointers: All numerical summaries above derive from archived analysis artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11/n10/n01/n00), analysis/condition_summary.csv (per‑condition counts), analysis/missingness_summary.csv, and provider accounting in deterministic_reconciliation.json. The paired bootstrap employed B = 10,000 and seed = 1729 (analysis log archived). Repair prompts, repaired outputs, and per‑episode validator traces are included in the evidence bundle to permit targeted replay and failure‑mode inspection.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation given small discordant counts: The GVR pipeline produced a small absolute improvement (~1.88 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact McNemar decision rule the improvement did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). With few discordants the exact two‑sided McNemar test is discrete and conservative; the paired bootstrap percentile CI (reported as descriptive) excludes zero but is not the preregistered decision instrument. We therefore present both inferential summaries so readers can weigh formal hypothesis rejection against effect magnitude and uncertainty.

Operational implications and boundary conditions: The task corpus exhibited a high baseline first‑pass accuracy (~97.7%), leaving few failures for repair and producing infrequent repair invocations (6/300). In settings with lower first‑pass accuracy, broader verifier coverage, or different sampling policies, GVR could yield larger absolute improvements. The observed provider accounting shows repair overhead in this run was small, but per‑episode latency was not archived and the preregistered latency estimand could not be evaluated; timing instrumentation should be included in future runs to measure operational cost.

Threats to validity: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate validator‑triggered repair for a fixed sample but do not measure the effect of alternative first‑pass strategies (multiple draws, constrained prompts) that were not executed. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite archived rule battery; violations outside that battery remain undetected. External validity: tasks derive from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor dialects; results do not generalize automatically to other vendors, larger topologies, or production heterogeneity. Conclusion validity: 34 both‑arm provider failures reduced the analysed sample from 300 to 266 and low discordant counts limit power to detect small absolute improvements.

Design recommendations grounded in artifacts: (1) When baseline pass rates are high, consider experiments that vary first‑pass sampling (e.g., independent multiple draws or constrained prompting arms) to increase discordant counts and power; such arms require independent initial samples and a separate preregistration. (2) Archive per‑episode timing (generation→validation→repair→final validation) to evaluate latency against operational bounds; our run lacked this instrumentation. (3) Expand validator rule coverage and publish validator test suites so verifier false negatives can be audited using per‑episode validator traces. (4) For deployment assessments include workload corpora with lower baseline accuracy or realistic operator‑created intents to better measure marginal repair yield.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini initial candidate + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Across 266 analysed pairs the guarded pipeline improved verifier pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α = 0.05 decision rule (p = 0.0625). A paired bootstrap percentile CI (B = 10,000, seed = 1729) reported descriptively excludes zero, illustrating finite‑sample interpretive differences when discordants are few. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per analysed pair = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and thus the preregistered latency estimand could not be evaluated. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived to enable reanalysis and targeted audits. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate estimand, the observed marginal benefit of a bounded automated repair is small on a high‑first‑pass corpus; larger benefits are plausible on corpora with lower baseline accuracy or with alternative first‑pass strategies that require separate preregistered arms. The run clarifies how deterministic verification and bounded automated repair interact with stochastic generation under reproducible experimental constraints and provides artifact‑grounded evidence for future methodological design choices.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (concise): Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json archived; declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration: cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Initial master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: before the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; after the autonomy lock the registered pipeline autonomously performed literature selection, preregistration, experimental execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI peer review simulation, and revision. Nondeterminism disclosure: execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset) and no deterministic sampling seed for provider calls is archived; therefore nondeterministic sampling of model outputs cannot be excluded for the recorded provider calls. Execution and analysis artifacts, logs, and hash manifests are archived in the evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N = 300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule (deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490), reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10 = 5, n01 = 0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and statistical power is limited.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
